lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s 101 on trade and tariffs
lead.head: Trade 101, for a world on the boil

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 95

play.label: Hear the case for open trade

body: For weeks, lis­ten­ers had asked Amit Varma and Ajay Shah for an episode on Donald Trump’s tar­iffs and the trade wars. Varma’s first in­stinct was that the two had al­ready said it all, over decades of writ­ing and think­ing.

But peo­ple con­sume their work piece­meal, he said. So the hosts set out to build a 101: why glob­al­i­sa­tion is good and tar­iffs are bad, from first prin­ci­ples, and how trade, and think­ing about it, evolved through his­tory.
The chaos of the present was left for the next episode.
Shah framed the stakes. Economics, pop­ulism, trade and in­ter­na­tional re­la­tions were “com­ing to­gether into a boil”, he said. “What hap­pens here will mat­ter for many many years to come.”
## Seven rea­sons

Varma brought seven rea­sons why glob­al­i­sa­tion is great, rea­sons both hosts hold. The first was moral, and he ex­pected many to re­ject it: “If you and I want to as­so­ciate with each other in any way that is vol­un­tary, who is any­body else to stop us?” {095-C01}

The next four were eco­nomic. Voluntary trade is pos­i­tive-sum, so buyer and seller both say thank you. Comparative ad­van­tage means a coun­try need not be the best at any­thing to gain, Shah said, be­cause what counts is the ratio of su­pe­ri­or­ity.
A big­ger mar­ket brings scale and spe­cial­i­sa­tion. And growth spreads across bor­ders, as one country’s ris­ing mid­dle class be­comes another’s mar­ket.

The last two were cul­tural. Everything Indians con­sider their own, Varma ar­gued, from food and clothes to lan­guages, came from some­where else. {095-C08} The potato, the chilli and the guava ar­rived through the Columbian Exchange.
The sev­enth, Shah’s, built on Jagdish Bhagwati: a closed econ­omy sets its elites fight­ing over a fixed pie, while an open one points them at the world.
## A his­tory with a warn­ing
The his­tory ran from the Silk Road, through colo­nial trade that was not re­ally free, to the mer­can­tilists, who hoarded gold and saw im­ports as gold sent away.
Adam Smith and David Ricardo flipped the frame. A coun­try ex­ports, Shah said, only so that it can im­port the won­ders of the world. {095-C11}

By 1909 the first wave of glob­al­i­sa­tion seemed so set­tled that Norman Angell de­clared war im­pos­si­ble. The First World War fol­lowed. After the Smoot-Hawley tar­iffs of 1930, Shah traced lines all the way to the sec­ond.

India’s own story ran from decades of im­port sub­sti­tu­tion to the open­ing of 1991. Shah called the four­fold rise in GDP from 1991 to 2011 India’s great­est eco­nomic achieve­ment in 10,000 years.
## Four myths, busted

The hosts then took apart four myths. Exporters do not pay tar­iffs; a country’s own con­sumers do. A trade deficit is ac­count­ing, not a loss. Tariffs hurt the very in­dus­tries they claim to pro­tect. And goods are no more spe­cial than ser­vices.

On most of what the Trump ad­min­is­tra­tion does, Varma said, there are rea­son­able ar­gu­ments on both sides. Not here. “On tar­iffs on this stuff, there is ab­so­lutely no ar­gu­ment on the other side.” {#noargument}
His own pol­icy would be sim­ple: India should take its tar­iffs to zero on ev­ery­thing, what­ever other coun­tries do, be­cause a tar­iff hurts a country’s own peo­ple. {095-C15}
For home­work, Varma pre­scribed Thomas Sowell’s *Basic Economics* and Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*. Shah named a sin­gle book: Jagdish Bhagwati’s *In Defense of Globalization*.

second.label: The first globalisation
second.head: The war that couldn’t be
second.deck: Norman Angell said trade had made war impossible. The next decade disagreed

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the book that ruled out war

body: The first wave of glob­al­i­sa­tion, built on the ideas of Adam Smith and David Ricardo, seemed set­tled. In 1909 Norman Angell ar­gued in *The Great Illusion* that war was now im­pos­si­ble, be­cause na­tions were too in­ter­twined by trade. {095-R10}

Amit Varma asked lis­ten­ers to mark the date. The First World War fol­lowed. John Maynard Keynes re­called the lost world in *The Economic Consequences of the Peace*: in 1914 a Londoner could order the prod­ucts of the whole earth by tele­phone, sip­ping his morn­ing tea. {095-R09}

The war made peo­ple cyn­i­cal and led to dis­as­trous decades, Varma said. The mis­take was be­liev­ing that free trade was now a done deal, and he ad­mit­ted that he and Ajay Shah had be­lieved it too. {095-S07}

quote.text: You thought the game was over, this is set­tled, this is good for hu­man­ity, didn’t work out that way.

third.head: The bus the tigers caught

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the bus India missed

body: Around 1950, Amit Varma said, India was doing re­ally well com­pared with South Korea and Taiwan. “We should have been the ones who suc­ceeded, who had em­braced democ­racy, who had so many good things going for them.” {095-S03}
But India kept its mar­kets closed. The East Asian Tigers opened theirs, achieved economies of scale and, com­pet­ing with the rest of the world, lifted their stan­dards. They took off.

Through the 1960s and 1970s, Varma said, India could have used its cheap labour for man­u­fac­tur­ing at scale. It missed the bus be­cause of ter­ri­ble labour laws and ter­ri­ble in­dus­trial laws. {#missedbus} Bangladesh, he said, is win­ning today be­cause it em­braced that path.
India later found a niche in ser­vices, partly be­cause it had many English-educated peo­ple for out­sourc­ing jobs.

p2.title: The case for trade
p2.deck: Seven reasons, a short history and four myths, in Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s 101

from1.head: Trade 101, for a world on the boil

quote.text: Every vol­un­tary ac­tion be­tween two con­sent­ing adults is al­ways a pos­i­tive sum game.

box.title: Ajay Shah’s one book
box.text: Jagdish Bhagwati’s *In Defense of Globalization* is the one book Ajay Shah names on the sub­ject. Bhagwati’s work with Srinivasan and Krueger also lies be­hind Shah’s ar­gu­ment that open­ness calms a country’s quar­relling elites. {095-R05}

sections.label: The first reasons
sections.head: Who is the state to stop us?
sections.caption: the freedom to trade
body: Amit Varma of­fered seven rea­sons why glob­al­i­sa­tion is great. The first, he said, is moral: if two peo­ple trade vol­un­tar­ily and no­body else’s rights are in­fringed, no­body has any busi­ness get­ting in the way, whether one is in India and the other in Washington, DC. {095-C01}

Ideologies are in­co­her­ent here, he said, de­fend­ing free­dom in the bed­room but not the mar­ket­place, or the re­verse. Ajay Shah wanted the point up front: call­ing Pune or Mozambique to strike a deal is the same act.
## Better at noth­ing, still bet­ter off

Every vol­un­tary trade is pos­i­tive-sum, Varma said, un­like ten­nis, where one player wins only if the other loses. The key word is vol­un­tary: colo­nial ex­trac­tion was not free trade. {095-C02}

To ex­plain com­par­a­tive ad­van­tage, Varma asked lis­ten­ers to as­sume Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma were the best driv­ers in Bombay. “Actually they’re not. I am,” he said. They should still hire a chauf­feur and keep their minds on cricket and act­ing. {095-J01}

Shah gave David Ricardo’s ver­sion: even if Portugal is bet­ter than England at both cloth and wine, both end up with more of each by spe­cial­is­ing and trad­ing. A poor coun­try, he said, need not be the world’s best at any­thing. {095-C03}

~ Scale was the fourth rea­son. With ten cus­tomers for shirts, Varma said, you get them made by hand; with the whole world, you can in­vest on a com­pletely dif­fer­ent scale, raise qual­ity and bring costs down. {#tenshirts}

quote.text: Every vol­un­tary ac­tion be­tween two con­sent­ing adults is al­ways a pos­i­tive sum game.

art.caption: Amit Varma on the freedom to trade

sections.label: The cultural case
sections.head: Imported, and all ours
sections.caption: why every culture is borrowed
body: Two of the seven rea­sons were cul­tural. Everything Indians con­sider quintessen­tially their own, Amit Varma said, from clothes to food to lan­guages, came from some­where else and melded to­gether. {095-C08}

The Silk Road car­ried re­li­gions along with goods. Islam, Varma said, did not first reach India with in­vaders: dur­ing the life­time of the Prophet Muhammad him­self, Muslims came to the south as traders. {095-S02}

The Columbian Exchange brought the potato, the chilli and the guava. Varma read from a World Economic Forum piece: “Imagine Italian cui­sine with­out toma­toes, which came from the new world, or Irish his­tory with­out the potato.” {095-J18}
## Fewer knives drawn

The sec­ond, Ajay Shah’s, was about po­lit­i­cal econ­omy, build­ing on Jagdish Bhagwati, Srinivasan and Krueger. In a closed econ­omy, he said, elites see a fi­nite land­scape and fight to grab a slice of the pie. {095-C09}
Open it up, and the game be­comes the world. Elites see eye to eye on poli­cies that make the coun­try strong, and the lev­els of con­flict go down.
~ Better things get done, Shah said, be­cause elites com­pete in a pos­i­tive way “rather than in a neg­a­tive way of try­ing to put the knife into each other”.

quote.text: It would be such a shal­low world if we be­come like North Korea, put up a high wall, and get stuck in one cul­ture.

art.caption: Amit Varma on why every culture is borrowed

sections.label: The history of ideas
sections.head: Kings who hoarded gold
sections.caption: mercantilism and Adam Smith
body: From the 16th to the 18th cen­tury, Amit Varma said, trade was seen through mer­can­tilist eyes. A king wanted gold and sil­ver in his trea­sury, so ex­ports were good, im­ports bad, and the aim was al­ways a sur­plus. Donald Trump, he said, holds that view today.
Even the age of ex­plo­ration did not bring free trade. Colonialism made it ex­trac­tive: for a long, long time, Spanish America could trade freely only with Spain. {#spanish}
In America, Alexander Hamilton, “a bit of a mer­can­tilist”, pop­u­larised the case for pro­tect­ing in­fant in­dus­tries; Jefferson, Varma said, was “more of a free­dom guy”. {095-J15}
## Wonders from over­seas

Ajay Shah ex­plained the turn. England grasped that the priv­i­lege of trade lies in buy­ing from oth­ers, and that a coun­try ex­ports to earn the means to im­port. His Casio wrist­watch, bought for all of 1,100 ru­pees, would not have been pos­si­ble with­out the abil­ity to buy from over­seas. {#casio}
Varma, who dis­trusts the great-man the­ory of his­tory, made an ex­cep­tion for Adam Smith. “Adam Smith is to eco­nom­ics, what Charles Darwin is to bi­ol­ogy,” Shah said. {095-J13}
~ In 1843, Varma added, *The Economist* was founded to de­fend free trade. It still calls it­self a news­pa­per, he noted, “for some rea­son”. {095-J10}

quote.text: There’s no fun in ex­port­ing. The real fun is in im­port­ing.

sections.label: The India story
sections.head: Opened up, grew fourfold
sections.caption: India’s opening up
body: For decades, Amit Varma said, India was com­pletely closed, be­cause its lead­ers be­lieved it must be self-reliant. The idea, he said, was then called im­port sub­sti­tu­tion.

What Nehru did and what Modi is doing are much the same, he said: “one is a suc­ces­sor of the other in terms of bad eco­nomic think­ing. In other ways they are very, very, very dif­fer­ent.” {095-J07}

Then came 1991. From then until 2008, Ajay Shah said, India only re­duced its trade bar­ri­ers and cap­i­tal con­trols, and it got the best eco­nomic per­for­mance in its his­tory. The con­nec­tion, he ar­gued, is causal, not ran­dom. {095-C19}
## A free­dom story

Varma stressed that the golden years strad­dle par­ties. The Congress kick­started them under Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh, the Vajpayee gov­ern­ment got many things right, and gov­ern­ments after 2008 got many things wrong.
Growth, he ar­gued, is a moral mat­ter. Their friend Nitin Pai reck­oned each 1 per cent rise in GDP takes a mil­lion peo­ple out of poverty, later re­vis­ing it to two mil­lion. {095-C07}
~ “It is okay for elites to sit in their air con­di­tioned rooms sip­ping their sin­gle malt to talk about ne­olib­eral val­ues,” Varma said. Growth, he said, is what puts food on plates. {095-J08}

quote.text: The great­est ever eco­nomic achieve­ment of India in the last 10,000 years was the 4x gain of GDP that hap­pened from 1991 to 2011.

art.caption: Amit Varma on India’s opening up

sections.label: Busting myths
sections.head: The foreigner doesn’t pay
sections.caption: who really pays a tariff
body: Donald Trump says for­eign­ers pay the tar­iffs. Ajay Shah had never heard the idea in his life, he said, “until one low IQ American pres­i­dent said it”. {095-J04}
A 100-rupee part comes into India, the gov­ern­ment charges a 10 per cent tar­iff, and it sells for 110 ru­pees. The Indian con­sumer pays. {095-C13}
Nor does it stop there. If a 500-rupee for­eign shirt be­comes 550, Shah said, every Indian maker of the same shirt will charge 550 too.
## A tax on your own poor

For Amit Varma, tar­iffs are al­ways a tax on a country’s own poor. Every in­ter­fer­ence in free mar­kets, by what he jok­ingly calls Varma’s law, moves wealth from the poor to the rich. In his ex­am­ple, a local maker pleads with the gov­ern­ment: “See, I’m cry­ing, I’m an in­fant, pro­tect me.” {095-J05}
So “re­cip­ro­cal” tar­iffs make no sense. Varma quoted the econ­o­mist Joan Robinson: other coun­tries putting rocks in their har­bours is no rea­son to put rocks in ours. {#robinson}
~ He would take India’s tar­iffs to zero on ev­ery­thing, what­ever oth­ers do. It is not about the other coun­try, he said, but about its own peo­ple. {095-C15}

quote.text: A tar­iff is an at­tack on your own peo­ple.

art.caption: Amit Varma on who really pays a tariff

sections.label: More myths
sections.head: In the red with the babysitter
sections.caption: trade deficits and services
body: The word deficit sounds like a loss, Ajay Shah said, but in trade it is arith­metic. In the mar­ket for toma­toes, the toma­toes bought al­ways equal the toma­toes sold, after the event. So it is in the mar­ket for dol­lars.

A for­eigner buys Indian shares, an Indian buys a house in London, Amit Varma im­ports cans of Diet Coke. Capital flows and trade flows must add up to zero, so an in­vest­ment boom that brings cap­i­tal in brings a trade deficit with it. {095-C16}
Varma added that in­di­vid­u­als trade, not coun­tries. Tim Harford has a trade deficit with his babysit­ter: he pays her, she buys noth­ing from him, and both are bet­ter off. {095-R14}
## Bearings and call cen­tres
Shah had never un­der­stood the ap­peal of goods. Some peo­ple, he said, have an “al­most mys­ti­cal at­tach­ment to goods” be­cause you can touch and feel a car. {#mystical}

Before fibre-optic ca­bles, ser­vices could not be traded; now they can, so global law firms should work in India and Indian firms abroad. “There is no rea­son to think that a ball bear­ing is some­how bet­ter or su­pe­rior than a call cen­tre call,” he said. {095-C18}
~ Varma agreed, but feared Donald Trump would take the les­son to tar­iff ser­vices too. “And it will be your fault,” he told Shah. {095-J06}

quote.text: It’s an ac­count­ing fact that if you have cap­i­tal com­ing into a coun­try, you will al­ways have a deficit on the trade ac­count.

art.caption: Amit Varma on trade deficits and services

quote.text: It is very im­por­tant to see trade not just as a lovely way to har­ness com­par­a­tive ad­van­tage and pros­per­ity, but also to stop the mad­ness of na­tion­al­ism and war

p3.title: Stories of trade
p3.deck: A biryani trail, a slump made worse and the road to war

stories.kicker: Amit Varma, after Thomas Sowell, on the Great Depression
stories.head: Down to 6.3%, then the tariffs
body: In the pop­u­lar imag­i­na­tion, the Great Depression began with the stock mar­ket crash of October 1929. {#crash} Amit Varma, draw­ing on one of his favourite writ­ers, Thomas Sowell, told it dif­fer­ently.
The crash was an event, Varma said. People lost jobs and com­pa­nies shut down. But it was not what re­ally brought about the Depression.
A cou­ple of months after the crash, un­em­ploy­ment peaked at 9 per cent. {#unemp} Then it started to de­cline. By June 1930 it was down to 6.3 per cent.

That was when President Hoover de­cided to lift em­ploy­ment. His idea, Varma said, was “clas­si­cal zero sum mer­can­tilist Donald Trumpish think­ing”: put tar­iffs on the out­side world, and do­mes­tic man­u­fac­tur­ers would build more fac­to­ries and bring the jobs back.
So came the Smoot-Hawley tar­iffs. The world re­acted, as of course it would, with re­cip­ro­cal tar­iffs of its own, and a trade war fol­lowed in which ev­ery­body suf­fered.
“Within five months, the un­em­ploy­ment shoots back up to over ten per­cent, and for the rest of the nine­teen thir­ties, it is a dou­ble digit fig­ure,” Varma said. {095-S05}
America moved into the Great Depression and did not man­age to come out for a long time.

~ Sowell, now 94, had warned about Smoot-Hawley decades ago. Recording on 15 April, Varma re­ported that Sowell had just given an in­ter­view on Donald Trump’s tar­iffs. {#sowell94} Varma put Sowell’s mes­sage this way: “It’s the same damn thing hap­pen­ing again.”
stories.why: In Varma’s telling, the crash did not turn a down­turn into a decade of dis­as­ter; the pol­icy re­sponse did. Shah drew the les­son for trade wars: “An eye for an eye leaves the whole world blind.” {095-J12}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the tariffs behind the Depression

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a tariff war became a shooting war
stories.head: From tariff wall to world war
body: After Smoot-Hawley, Ajay Shah re­called, global trade fell by about 66 per cent. He drew lines from those tar­iffs all the way to the Second World War. {095-S06}
The first runs through pol­i­tics. Economic hard­ship de­stroys the cen­tre, he said, and peo­ple “go off into ex­trem­ist ide­olo­gies”, na­tional so­cial­ist on one side, com­mu­nist on the other.
The sec­ond runs through re­sources. If trade fails and you can­not buy the rare earths you need, Shah said, you start to think: “I will bloody march into Africa and I will con­quer Africa.” {#march}

~ After 1930 came a Japanese in­va­sion in 1931, Italy’s in­va­sion of Ethiopia in 1935 and Germany’s drive for Lebensraum. *Mein Kampf* pre­dates the tar­iffs, Shah noted, but they fed a German be­lief that the trad­ing sys­tem was British-controlled and that Germany must con­quer land to pros­per.

quote.text: There are lines that run from Smoot-Hawley all the way to the sec­ond world war.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the road from tariffs to war

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a food trip through Mysore and Mangalore
stories.head: Eight meals and a lesson in trade
body: Amit Varma once went on a food trip through Mysore and Mangalore with about 15 friends, many of whom Ajay Shah knows. They took a bus, listed their stops on an Excel sheet and ate some­thing like eight meals a day.
In one area, within a five-kilometre ra­dius of Mangalore, they found five dif­fer­ent kinds of biryani. All of them, Varma said, were au­then­tic to the place. {095-S01}
Each had arisen in its own way from the same lit­tle area. “This is beau­ti­ful,” Varma said. “This is what trade gives you.”

~ The trip closed the first of his cul­tural ar­gu­ments for glob­al­i­sa­tion, that ev­ery­thing Indians eat, wear and say came from else­where. That cul­tural rea­son, he said, might even be the strong­est.
stories.why: What we call au­then­tic local food is the lay­ered re­sult of ex­change. Globalisation, in Varma’s telling, shows up in one small area near Mangalore, not just in ab­stract trade sta­tis­tics. {095-C08}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on five biryanis near Mangalore

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the would-be businessmen of his youth
stories.head: Business plan: befriend the state
body: Jagdish Bhagwati once ob­served that in China people’s men­tal­ity is profit-seeking, while in India it is rent-seeking. {#bhagwati} Amit Varma and a for­mer col­league of Ajay Shah’s once planned to write a piece about it.
Profit-seeking, Varma ex­plained, means mak­ing money by bring­ing value to some­one else in a dou­ble thank-you mo­ment. Rent-seeking is ex­trac­tive, such as using a mo­nop­oly the state holds.
In all his young years, he said, when­ever he met some­one who wanted to start a busi­ness, he was often shocked by their ex­ploita­tive mind­set. {095-S04}

~ After decades of a closed econ­omy, the path to pros­per­ity ran through the state. Either you be­came part of it, or you be­came its crony and got it to put tar­iffs on your com­peti­tors or cre­ate entry bar­ri­ers.

quote.text: If you are open, then you are com­pet­ing in the global mar­ket­place and you’ll have a profit seek­ing men­tal­ity.

quiz.q: Why should Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma hire a chauffeur, even if they drive best?
quiz.a: Their time and minds are worth more spent on cricket and act­ing.

quiz.q: In David Ricardo’s example, what did England and Portugal make and trade?
quiz.a: Cloth and wine; by spe­cial­is­ing, both coun­tries end up with more of each.

quiz.q: What did Norman Angell argue in *The Great Illusion*, published in 1909?
quiz.a: That war was now im­pos­si­ble, since na­tions were too in­ter­twined by trade.

quiz.q: A 100-rupee import carries a 10 per cent tariff and sells for 110. Who pays the extra?
quiz.a: The Indian con­sumer. Exporters don’t pay tar­iffs; a country’s own buy­ers do.

quiz.q: Whose trade deficit with his babysitter shows that a deficit need not mean a loss?
quiz.a: Tim Harford’s. He pays her, she buys noth­ing from him, and both gain.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 95. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Thomas Sowell (Internet Archive Book Images, public domain); Jagdish Bhagwati (Johannes Jansson, CC BY 2.5 dk); David Ricardo (Thomas Phillips, public domain); Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Alexander Hamilton (John Trumbull, public domain); Manmohan Singh (India, GODL-India); P. V. Narasimha Rao (Christian Lambiotte - European Commission, CC BY 4.0); Joan Robinson (W. Punt for Anefo, CC0); Tim Harford (PopTech, CC BY-SA 2.0); John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Basic Economics
shelf.creator: Thomas Sowell
shelf.why: Sowell’s book for learn­ing the basic con­cepts of eco­nom­ics in sim­ple lan­guage, one of Amit’s go-to an­swers when asked for a sin­gle fun­da­men­tal book; he says to read all of Sowell’s books.

shelf.title: Applied Economics
shelf.creator: Thomas Sowell
shelf.why: Part of Amit’s ad­vice to read ev­ery­thing Sowell has writ­ten.

shelf.title: Economics in One Lesson
shelf.creator: Henry Hazlitt
shelf.why: Hazlitt’s 1946 ‘col­lec­tion of light bulbs’ that uses the ba­sics of scarcity and in­cen­tives to clear up fal­la­cies about price con­trols, tar­iffs, in­fla­tion and gov­ern­ment spend­ing, teach­ing you to ask what the money would have done if left with con­sumers.

shelf.title: Everything by Frédéric Bastiat (show notes link: Timeless Essays on Political Economy)
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: The writ­ings of ‘the man who re­ally turned me on to freedom’, as Amit puts it: Bastiat put com­plex eco­nomic ideas into sim­ple lan­guage with­out dumb­ing them down, and gives you a frame­work for see­ing the world.

shelf.title: In Defense of Globalization
shelf.creator: Jagdish Bhagwati
shelf.why: Ajay’s sin­gle go-to book on glob­al­i­sa­tion, which Amit calls mag­nif­i­cent and the nat­u­ral com­pan­ion to Ajay’s case for it; Bhagwati’s work also un­der­lies the hosts’ ar­gu­ments on rent-seeking.

shelf.title: The Wealth of Nations
shelf.creator: Adam Smith
shelf.why: The found­ing text on how na­tions be­come pros­per­ous: Ajay says Smith is to eco­nom­ics what Darwin is to bi­ol­ogy, and it is ‘eerie’ how much he got right.

shelf.title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
shelf.creator: Adam Smith
shelf.why: Smith’s often-overlooked philo­soph­i­cal mas­ter­piece, which coined the ‘man of system’, the plan­ner who treats peo­ple like chess pieces: the best warn­ing against Maoist-style grand de­signs.

shelf.title: Conversation and Society (Episode 182, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Russ Roberts
shelf.why: Russ Roberts on the art of con­ver­sa­tion and Adam Smith’s moral phi­los­o­phy, an episode Amit re­mem­bers for its ‘mag­i­cal chemistry’.

shelf.title: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
shelf.creator: John Maynard Keynes
shelf.why: Keynes’s vivid record of how glob­alised the pre-war world was and what war de­stroyed.

shelf.title: The Great Illusion
shelf.creator: Norman Angell
shelf.why: Worth know­ing as a cau­tion­ary tale.

shelf.title: Thomas Sowell interviewed by Peter Robinson
shelf.creator: Peter Robinson with Thomas Sowell
shelf.why: Sowell, who wrote about Smoot-Hawley decades ago, says today’s tar­iffs are the same thing hap­pen­ing again.

shelf.title: I, Pencil
shelf.creator: Leonard Read
shelf.why: A pen­cil nar­rates its own mak­ing from ma­te­ri­als and know-how scat­tered across many coun­tries, co­or­di­nated by prices with no one in charge.

shelf.title: The Double ‘Thank You’ Moment
shelf.creator: John Stossel
shelf.why: Stossel’s sim­plest pic­ture of pos­i­tive-sum ex­change: when you buy a cof­fee, you thank the barista and the barista thanks you, be­cause both are bet­ter off.

shelf.title: A trade deficit with a babysitter
shelf.creator: Tim Harford
shelf.why: Harford al­ways pays his babysit­ter and she buys noth­ing from him, yet both are bet­ter off: a neat de­mo­li­tion of panic about bi­lat­eral trade deficits and of the mis­lead­ing word ‘deficit’.

shelf.title: A brief history of globalization
shelf.creator: Peter Vanham
shelf.why: A con­cise over­view of how trade re­shaped what the world eats: imag­ine Italian cui­sine with­out toma­toes, or Irish his­tory with­out the potato.

shelf.title: India’s Problem is Poverty, Not Inequality
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit sep­a­rates two prob­lems peo­ple rou­tinely con­fuse and that need op­po­site so­lu­tions: in a pos­i­tive-sum world in­equal­ity can rise while poverty falls, as in India after 1991, so end­ing poverty through growth is the real moral im­per­a­tive.

shelf.title: The Great Redistribution
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that mar­ket in­ter­ven­tions such as tar­iffs or bans on FDI in re­tail qui­etly move money from many dis­persed, poor con­sumers to a few or­gan­ised, rich in­ter­est groups, the op­po­site of their stated in­ten­tion.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left un­done (fac­tor mar­kets, agri­cul­ture), and how free­ing parts of the econ­omy set off the dis­cov­ery and trade be­hind India’s growth spurt.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.title: How to Do Development (Episode 57, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: Nothing is Indian! Everything is Indian! (Episode 12, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: One of the show’s most pop­u­lar episodes: al­most ev­ery­thing we con­sider quintessen­tially Indian, from food to clothes to lan­guages, came from else­where and blended to­gether, so get­ting na­tion­al­is­tic about it is ridicu­lous.

shelf.title: Pushpesh Pant Feasts on the Buffet of Life (Episode 326, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pushpesh Pant
shelf.why: A re­mark­able con­ver­sa­tion in which Pushpesh Pant urges Indians to ex­plore their own country’s food di­ver­sity, shar­ing the imag­ined maps in his head (re­gions mapped by their sour­ing agent) and how ‘clas­si­cally Indian’ in­gre­di­ents came from out­side.

shelf.title: The Indianness of Indian Food (Episode 95, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Doctor
shelf.why: Vikram Doctor, whom Amit calls the world’s best food writer, on how Indian cui­sine is built from im­ported in­gre­di­ents such as the potato, the chilli and the guava.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case that in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion is the en­gine of growth: com­pet­ing with the world forces firms to im­port best prac­tices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the econ­omy.

shelf.title: The Art of Podcasting (Episode 49, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s fullest think­ing on the craft of pod­cast­ing, which Ajay says also ex­plains how the mod­ern media and cre­ative economies work.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 54, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Decades of both hosts’ think­ing on ed­u­ca­tion packed into about an hour, an episode Amit is proud of.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Episode 25, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on mar­ket fail­ure in its pre­cise tech­ni­cal sense (pub­lic goods, ex­ter­nal­i­ties and the rest) and on the nar­row con­di­tions under which the state may in­ter­vene, con­di­tions that are nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient.

shelf.title: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Episode 46, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On be­liefs im­ported from rich-world dis­course that make their hold­ers feel vir­tu­ous while hurt­ing the peo­ple they claim to help, such as the min­i­mum wage, or op­pos­ing sweat­shops that beat every other op­tion work­ers have.

laughs.text: Amit takes over the com­par­a­tive-advantage ex­am­ple from Ajay (‘Let me break this down be­cause you will find a way to mess it up’), then asks us to as­sume Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma are the best driv­ers in Bombay: ‘Actually they’re not. I am.’
Ajay on the claim that ex­porters pay tar­iffs: ‘I’ve never heard this idea in my whole life until one low IQ American pres­i­dent said it.’

After Ajay ar­gues goods and ser­vices are equal, Amit wor­ries Trump might con­clude: ‘Why should I put tar­iffs only on goods? I will also put tar­iffs on ser­vices. And it will be your fault, Ajay.’
The Economist was founded in 1843 to de­fend free trade and, as Amit notes, ‘still calls it­self a news­pa­per, by the way, for some rea­son.’
Marx and Engels, in Amit’s view, got the de­scrip­tion right and the anal­y­sis wrong: ‘na­tional one-sidedness and nar­row-mindedness be­come more and more im­pos­si­ble.’
